A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same meta-reasoning benchmark study, renamed from DiagGSM8K to MR-GSM8k. The main text, tables, figures, equations and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including the image-based prompts and examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations on 3,000 annotated question-solution pairs, an in-domain fine-tuning experiment and a 100-instance assessment of automated grading.

after.justification: v3 retains original benchmark and fine-tuning results, revises several reported values and presents an expanded comparison of manual and automated grading in Appendix B.

M1.justification: The three diagnostic tasks, evaluation prompt, GPT4-based training-data generation and QLoRA fine-tuning procedure are retained. The appendix prompt images are identical. MR-Score changes evaluation aggregation rather than the model or diagnostic procedure.

E1.justification: Table 1 retains the same 1,418 original, 222 Program-of-Thought and 1,360 reversed examples. v3 Section 7 additionally reports trying solutions sampled from different generating models, adding a limited test scenario, although those models and sample sizes are unspecified.

E2.justification: The benchmark comparison retains Claude2, GPT3.5, GPT4, WizardMath-70B, Mammoth-70B, MetaMath-70B and the diagnostic fine-tuned llama2 model. Table 3 also retains the GSM8K-only llama2 control. Renaming llama2-70B-diag to llama2-70B-MR does not introduce another comparator.

E3.justification: v3 Section 3.2 replaces binary accuracy with MCC and introduces MR-Score, combining clipped MCC, error-step accuracy and error-reason accuracy with weights 0.2, 0.3 and 0.5. Automated-grader validation expands from a balanced 100-instance sample to a reported 1,668 judgments. The main zero-shot/three-shot settings and temperature 0.5 remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v1's small automated-grading confusion matrix becomes a broader validation of whether automatic grading preserves benchmark scores: v3 Appendix B adds per-model manual-versus-automatic comparisons and a larger confusion matrix. Section 7 also briefly reports checks using different solution generators. Existing prompt observations, fine-tuning analyses and appendix case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. The larger grading sample changes the evaluation design, without introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Results change beyond percentage formatting: under the same stated main settings, GPT4's correctly located error steps increase from 784/1573 to 823/1573, and complete diagnoses from 644/1573 to 677/1573. Other model counts also change, without an explanation of their origin. v3 additionally reports MCC, MR-Score and automated-grading results, including GPT4 manual/automatic MR-Scores of 0.495/0.512.

T1.justification: v3 introduces the mathematical definition of MR-Score, including zero-clipping MCC and weighting the three component scores, absent from v1. This is a limited addition of formal definitions; no theorem, proof or theoretical guarantee is added.

C1.justification: v3 explicitly adds MR-Score to the claimed contributions. The headline GPT4-versus-GPT3.5 advantage changes from approximately tenfold diagnostic success to fivefold performance measured by MR-Score. The central claims about meta-reasoning evaluation and weaknesses concealed by conventional benchmarks remain.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes caution about GPT4 grading because of false positives; v3 argues that it can serve as a useful automatic evaluator because aggregate MR-Scores closely match manual scores, while still encouraging manual annotation. v3 also adds an overfitting interpretation of output-format failures and expands the discussion of counterfactual reasoning and grounding. The limitation that diagnostic fine-tuning need not improve GSM8K performance is retained.

D1.justification: v3 specifies GPT4-Turbo-1106 as the automatic grader and documents the new scoring weights and clipping rule. Annotation procedures, evaluation and data-generation prompts, sampling temperatures and fine-tuning details were already supplied in v1; their relocation does not constitute new disclosure.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting automated judging, including Zheng et al. and Liu et al., alongside Matthews for MCC and Gudibande et al. for imitation limitations. Some alignment and stochastic-parrot references are removed. The main related-work discussion and positioning of meta-reasoning evaluation remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The title and benchmark terminology change, and the introduction is substantially shortened and reorganized. Evaluation gains separate dataset and metric subsections; discussion and limitations are separated. Annotation procedures, fine-tuning implications and prompt discussions are redistributed into a reorganized appendix with additional subsections.

P2.justification: Tables 2 and 3 are redesigned around MCC and MR-Score, and a manual-versus-automatic comparison table is added. Figure 1 changes its axis and displayed metric; the benchmark schematic moves earlier, the reasoning-tree illustration moves to Discussion, and the confusion matrix moves to the appendix. Existing appendix prompt and example images are reused.

improvement.justification: The explicit scoring definition and per-model grading comparison make the benchmark easier to apply and provide evidence that automated grading preserves model rankings, improving on v1's preliminary 100-instance check. The gain is limited by unexplained changes in benchmark counts and an unresolved inconsistency: v3 Table 4 totals 1,692 step-correct judgments, whereas Table 5 summarizes 1,668.
